description.narrative:
Objectives The overall programme objective is to provide better living conditions to at least 200 000 Harare citizens by increasing their access to sustainable waste management services, clean energy provision and to promote energy and resource efficiency in Zimbabwe's Built Environment.
Outcome 1: Implement Sustainable Waste Management Practices in Greater Harare
This will be achieved through developing five integrated resource recovery facilities in strategic locations in Harare. They will serve as demonstrations of how waste can be managed, processed and sold and will create jobs and income earning opportunities for the communities. Connected to this activity is that of improving waste pickers working conditions and livelihoods and awareness raising and capacity building in waste management for the relevant authorities.
Outcome 2: Increased Access to Clean Energy by the Urban and Peri Urban Poor in Harare.
This will be achieved through the establishment of two multi-functional clean energy centres for women and youth empowerment. The centres will act as hubs for business training, business creation and provide access to energy, clean water and solar street lighting for surrounding communities. Further activities include hands on training sessions on renewable energy technologies for women and youth, conducting entrepreneurship capacity training and then providing seed capital to those trainee women and youth that have demonstrated strong potential.
Outcome 3: Achieved Energy and Resource Efficiencies in Zimbabwe's Built Environment
This will be achieved through developing a baseline on energy consumption across a sample of residential, commercial and industrial buildings, establishing a green building rating and certification system for Zimbabwe, setting standards for energy and resource efficiency for future construction, raising awareness when it comes to low carbon interventions in the building sector and creation of a carbon neutral brick production facility to act as a pilot and show the potential of climate smart building materials.
Job Creation
The project is expected to facilitate various levels of income-generating activities; these include the improved work efficiency and income of those involved in the waste management supply chain and energy generation and services. Several individuals, from unskilled to skilled laborers will be employed in the waste collection stream, the integrated resource recovery facility, the waste-to-energy power facility, and the multi-functional clean energy centres. The project is expected to generate at least 500 direct jobs within the project boundary. Through its wide adoption of the demonstrated interventions, the project is expected to result in creating income streams for at least 100,000 jobs in the next five years.

Harare Sustainable City Initiative (HSCI) är ett program i Zimbabwe, lett av UN-Habitat och finansierat av den svenska regeringen, som syftar till att förbättra medborgarnas välbefinnande genom att förbättra tillgången till hållbara städer, cirkulär ekonomi och avfallshantering, ren energi och resurseffektiva byggmaterial.

The Harare Sustainable City Initiative (HSCI) is a program in Zimbabwe, led by UN-Habitat and funded by the Swedish Government, that aims to improve citizens' well-being by enhancing access to sustainable urban services, promoting waste-to-wealth systems, clean energy, and resource-efficient building materials.

description.narrative:
Background
During year 2025, the implementation of the project recovered from the severe delays and challenges met in the previous year of 2024. The replacement of the project manager in Nairobi to a senior project manager based in Harare together with the fast-track turn-over workplan enabled major achievements during 2025 which compensated for some of the time lost. A surge team was established in Harare to speed- up the work in October 2024 and UN-habitat replaced the project manager in Nairobi, with a person who is based on the ground in Zimbabwe from the 13th of December 2024 to ensure that the challenges on the ground were addressed and to speed up processes and implementation of the programme. This person is a senior manager, with experience of construction project as well as capacity development/training. At the same time the surge team continued to provide support from the HQ office in Nairobi. The coordination between the UN-habitat HQ, UN-Habitat and implementing partners as well as other stakeholders have been enhanced by strengthen meetings of the PMU Unit, Steering Committee etc. At the end of year 2024 all the needed legal documents signed for the various sites and the MoUs were established and signed., which facilitated the construction of the various sites. This provided a good foundation for some of the examples of achievements in 2025 presented below.
Main project progress towards outcomes
Outcome 1: Sustainable Waste to Wealth Practices in Harare is established.
Outcome 1 includes a various of different outputs focusing on awareness building around sustainable waste. Public awareness campaigns and household-level outreach contributed to positive shifts in attitudes and practices around waste separation, recycling, and responsible disposal.
Capacity for structured waste management was strengthened in 2025 among waste reclaimers and community actors through targeted training led by Zimbabwe Sunshine Group. A total of 1,545 participants (1,054 women, 491 men, including 1,157 youth) were reached with training on integrated solid waste management, waste-to-wealth, occupational health and safety, and PSEA, improving skills in waste separation, safe handling, environmental responsibility, and participation in more organized waste systems.
Focus is also to improve informal waste workers wellbeing, working conditions and livelihoods. In 2025, Soberlife International expanded its intervention across Epworth, Highfields, Showgrounds, and TafaraMabvuku. These interventions included profiling, awareness, counselling, follow-up, and referral services addressing drug and substance abuse and mental wellbeing challenges affecting health, safety, and continuity in recovery work. A total of 142 waste pickers were profiled, 30 participants trained, 1,000 households reached, and 4 referrals made for rehabilitation support. In addition, a targeted training held on 30 April 2025 equipped 33 participants as Change Champions, who subsequently conducted door-to-door campaigns reaching 2,968 households. Complementary community platforms, including clean-up campaigns and a sobriety sports tournament reaching approximately 2,000 people, further expanded awareness and engagement.
One important output under this outcome is the establishment of four sustainable resources recovery facilities, based on the Integrated Resource Recovery Centres (IRRC) model.
Epworth: Phase 1 rehabilitation of the Epworth recycling plant was successfully completed, transforming a previously degraded and unsafe site into a stable, development-ready platform for the establishment of an Integrated Resource Recovery Centre (IRRC). The site, which had been characterized by deep gullies, waterlogging, and geotechnical instability due to uncontrolled extraction activities, was rehabilitated through levelling, backfilling, compaction, and dewatering. Led by the Green Building Council of Zimbabwe in partnership with UN-Habitat and the Epworth Local Board, these interventions restored land integrity, reduced environmental and safety risks, and laid the foundation for infrastructure development. Building on this foundation, Practical Action commenced construction of the IRRC in November 2025, with overall progress reaching an estimated 8090% completion by year-end.
From October to December 2025, the Practical Action, conducted extensive stakeholder engagement processes, Energy & Waste Baseline and Needs Assessment and viable business assessments across Highfields, Showgrounds, Mabvuku- Tafara, Epworth, and Glen View to strengthen the waste-to-wealth and clean energy components of HSCI. Through consultations with government ministries, local authorities, private sector actors, community-based organizations, and targeted communities, the exercise assessed implementation progress and identified key operational gaps, constraints, and opportunities. The findings generated actionable evidence that is now guiding the next phase of delivery, informing the development of inclusive business models, governance and ownership structures, and sustainability frameworks for the IRRCs and MCECs. This process strengthened the operational depth of implementation by clarifying how facilities can function within local economic and institutional contexts, reinforcing the link between infrastructure, local ownership, and long-term viability.
Outcome 2: Increase access to clean energy by the urban and peri-urban poor in Harare.
During the reporting period, a Multifunctional Clean Energy Centre (MCEC) in Mabvuku was completed and equipped with a 50kW solar PV system and 100kWh battery storage, designed to provide reliable, clean energy for women- and youth-led enterprises. The centre will support a range of productive-use businesses, including an ICT hub, energy shop, sewing, water services, and welding. By year-end, a sewing enterprise was fully operational, repurposing old clothes into reusable carrier bags sold within the community, generating income to sustain operations and support livelihoods.
To strengthen innovatin and circular economy linkages, UN-Habitat supported a pilot on the repair and repurpose of solar products, implemented by Action24 at the Mabvuku MCEC. The pilot addresses both the high cost of solar technologies and the growing environmental risks of solar E-waste by training youth technicians to collect, repair, and repurpose solar equipment for basic energy uses such as lighting and phone charging. A Bring-it-dont Burn itcampaign, and outreach to local repair and scrap networks reaching 850 individuals and 100 households (60% youth). In addition, three youths were trained as Trainers of Trainers to support skills transfer and scale-up.
Building on progress reported in the previous cycle, UN-Habitat advanced the establishment of the Mabvuku and Epworth MCECs. Foundational work included the development and approval of conceptual designs, detailed site layouts, and construction drawings by the City of Harare, alongside an Environmental Management Plan approved by the Environmental Management Agency, with Environmental Impact Assessments (EIA) certificates issued. During the current reporting period, construction of the Mabvuku MCEC was successfully completed, marking a major project milestone. The facility incorporates innovative construction approaches, including the repurposing of shipping containers for business units and offices, promoting resource efficiency and reducing the environmental footprint of construction.
The Mabvuku MCEC is powered by a 50kW solar PV system and 100kWh battery storage, providing reliable, clean, and affordable energy to support productive-use enterprises and minimize power disruptions. This strengthens business continuity and enhances economic productivity for users, particularly women and youth-led enterprises. In parallel, construction and equipping of the second MCEC in Epworth progressed during the reporting period and will be detailed further in the next cycle, maintaining momentum toward expanding access to clean energy infrastructure across target communities.
Outcome 3: Achieve energy and resource efficiencies in Zimbabwes built environment.
UN-Habitat is working with the implementing partner Green Building Council of Zimbabwe to promote local knowledge transfer and strengthening local capacity and development of green building solutions adopted to the local context and in alignment with Zimbabwes development agenda and priorities and international best practices.
During the reporting period, the Green Building Council of Zimbabwe, as the implementing partner, carried out a series of awareness and capacity-building activities focused on low-carbon interventions in the built sector in Zimbabwe. These activities include Capacity building workshop on Zimbabwes Energy Efficiency Code and Validation workshop for Decarbonizing the built Environment towards achieving set NDCs for Zimbabwe.
In July 2025, a policy and regulatory recommendations report was developed to advance energy and resource efficiency in Zimbabwes built environment, leveraging the Zimbabwe Green Building Rating and Certification System (Z-GBCS) as a central tool for driving sustainable construction and climate resilience. The report proposed a comprehensive framework combining regulatory measures, financial incentives, and capacity-building initiatives to strengthen building performance, support retrofitting of existing infrastructure, and integrate sustainability into national policies.
To build policy awareness and stakeholder alignment, UN-Habitat and the Green Building Council of Zimbabwe convened a series of high-level engagements. A one-day workshop held on 9 May 2025 in Harare brought together 35 participants from Parliament, government ministries, the private sector, academia, and the media to strengthen understanding of sustainable building practices and policy integration. Discussions highlighted gaps in existing regulatory frameworks and emphasized the need for stronger coordination, compliance tools, enforcement mechanisms, and incentives. A follow-up session on 13 June 2025 engaged 26 stakeholders, including members of the Senate Thematic Committee on Climate Change, to explore how legislation can accelerate climate-smart construction. These dialogues reinforced political will and provided clear direction for integrating sustainability into national policy and legislative processes.
